title: What Is a Chaebol? The Word Behind Samsung, Hyundai and Korea's Family Empires
html:
Samsung, SK, Hyundai, LG, Lotte. When English-language news talks about these groups, it often uses one Korean word: chaebol (재벌).

In one line

A chaebol is a large South Korean business group made up of many affiliated companies and run and controlled by a founding family.

Where the word comes from

The word is written 財閥 in Chinese characters: chae (財) means wealth and beol (閥) means a clan or faction. So a chaebol is, literally, a "wealth clan." The same two characters are read zaibatsu in Japanese, the name for the family conglomerates that dominated Japan from the Meiji era until 1945, and many Korean groups modeled themselves on them. Merriam-Webster dates the English use of "chaebol" to at least 1972.

How the chaebol got so big

After Park Chung-hee took power in 1961, the government pushed growth through a small number of large companies, giving them cheap credit and export targets. The groups expanded into everything from ships and cars to insurance and department stores.

The 1997 Asian financial crisis broke that model. Korea needed an IMF bailout of more than 50 billion dollars, and many of the 30 largest groups went under (sources differ on the exact count). In 1999 Daewoo collapsed with debts of roughly 80 billion dollars, at the time the largest corporate bankruptcy in history.

How much of the economy?

Figures vary by method, but the scale is clear. Wikipedia, citing 2023 data, puts the combined revenue of the top four groups (Samsung, SK, Hyundai and LG) at about 40% of South Korea's GDP. The Council on Foreign Relations noted in 2018 that Samsung Electronics alone had been worth more than 14% of GDP over the previous decade.

In the news

The word shows up most often in stories about corporate governance. Families often control a whole group while owning only a small slice of it, through chains of affiliates holding shares in each other. Critics say this lets owners favor family interests over ordinary shareholders, and it is one of the reasons given for the "Korea discount" in Korean stock prices. On November 1, 2026, the Korea Exchange publicly named 151 companies with persistently low valuations, including affiliates of several big groups such as Hanwha, Hyundai and Lotte.

Don't confuse it with

  • Zaibatsu: the Japanese groups were broken up after World War II. Korea's chaebol are still family-led today.
  • Keiretsu: Japan's postwar business networks, linked around banks rather than one controlling family.
  • A Western conglomerate: often owned by many shareholders with no single family in charge.

Sources
